title.narrative: UNDP, National Demobilization and Reintegration Programme in Ethiopia
UNDP, National Demobilization and Reintegration Programme in Ethiopia

description.narrative: Outcome A total of 371,971 ex-combatants (XCs) from conflict-impacted Tigray and other regions are demobilized, the military command structure is broken, and XCs are inserted back into their communities as civilians to build a lasting peace, enable reconciliation and reinforce social cohesion. 75,000 XCs are demobilized in 2024, and the remaining are demobilized in 2025/2026. XCs will be reinserted back to their communities in the period 2024-2026. Those in need will be supported with medical care SGBV services, MHPSS and disability support.

Denna insats för avväpning, demobilisering och återintegrering av före detta soldater från kriget i Tigray (DDR ­ Disarmament, Demobilisation and Reintegration) syftar till att spela en viktig roll i att skapa förtroende för genomförbarheten i ”fredsavtalet” (Cessession of Hostilities Agreement, CoHA) mellan den federala regeringen i Etiopien och TPLF (Tigray Peoples’ Liberation Front). Inte minst för direkt berörda aktörer såsom ex­kombattanter och internflyktingar. En demobilisering av soldater och återintegrering av dessa till lokalsamhällen i Tigray via olika program, motverkar risken att dessa återgår till stridigheter, och bidrar därmed till ökad stabilitet i regionen. Ett väl genomfört DDR program ökar lokalsamhällenas trygghet och säkerhet, bidrar till minskade spänningar och bildar en bas för långsiktigt hållbar fred genom att före detta soldater återgår till produktiv sysselsättning i samhället och därmed bidrar till att återbygga och utveckla sina lokalsamhällen.

This contribution aims to implement the DDR process, and plays a crucial role in building trust in the viability of the CoHA peace agreement. Not least among those directly implicated such as excombatants and IDPs. The demobilizing of combatants, and reintegrating them in to society through various programs, help prevent the resurgence of armed groups and establish stability in the region. By successfully implementing the DDR process, communities can experience increased security, reduced tensions and start to build a foundation for sustainable peace as former combatants become productive members of society, contributing to the rebuilding and development of their communities.

title.narrative: UNDP, National Demobilization and Reintegration Programme in Ethiopia
UNDP, National Demobilization and Reintegration Programme in Ethiopia

description.narrative:
Scale-up of DDR: The national DDR process moved into a significantly larger implementation phase in 2025, with 72,955 ex-combatants (XCs) demobilized across Tigray, Oromia, Afar and Amhara. This brought the cumulative number of demobilized XCs to 80,908, compared with 7,953 demobilized in 2024, making it one of the largest DDR programmes currently under implementation in Africa. The programme also facilitated reinsertion payments of ETB 90,400 per XC for 75,746 XCs, amounting to approximately ETB 6.8 billion (USD 53 million), providing immediate financial support following demobilization.
National DDR systems Strengthened: In 2025, a further 30 national and regional NRC staff and partners were trained, bringing the total number trained through the programme to 67. The DREAM database was also transferred to and adopted by the NRC as a core tool for XC registration, profiling and case management, with all 80,908 demobilized XCs registered in the system.
Reintegration framework: The programme began establishing the systems needed to move from large-scale demobilization to longer-term reintegration. The NRC drafted a National Reintegration Framework in consultation with regional governments, providing a common basis for reintegration planning. In Tigray, the programme also assessed reintegration needs across five woredas and mapped 190 existing initiatives that could serve as referral pathways for XCs, creating an evidence base for linking demobilised XCs with employment, skills development and other services.
Inclusivity: The programme strengthened the capacity of the DDR process to respond to the specific needs of women, youth and persons with disabilities. 12,070 women were demobilised, while 76% of XCs were between 18 and 32 years old. Gender-responsive measures included nutritional support for lactating mothers and gender equality training for government staff. Approximately 42,923 XCs were registered as having disabilities, with specialised support provided through psychosocial services and MHPSS training for 320 persons with disabilities, including 35 women, and 10 caretakers. The programme also initiated the procurement of assistive devices and assessed the skills, employment and service needs of XCs with disabilities to inform their reintegration.
Strengthened DDR data management: The Disarmament, Demobilization and Reintegration (DDR) Information Management System (DREAM) evolved into the backbone of Ethiopias national DDR programme, supporting registration, case management, beneficiary profiling, reintegration planning, and reporting. Enhanced biometric verification and data management functions improved data quality, accountability, and programme oversight, while regular analytical reporting enabled evidence-based planning and decision-making. By the end of the reporting period, DREAM had been successfully scaled to support the registration and management of more than 80,000 ex-combatants, reflecting strengthened institutional capacity and national ownership.
Community recovery: The programme linked DDR with recovery in conflict-affected communities by investing USD 1.17 million in 29 infrastructure rehabilitation initiatives. These interventions strengthened the capacity of local institutions and service providers, including civil servants and medical personnel, and restored access to essential services for more than one million community members. This provided a complementary community-level dimension to the individual support provided through DDR.
Independent monitoring and early DDR outcomes: The programme completed its first independent rapid assessment of demobilized ex-combatants in Tigray, providing initial evidence of programme results. The assessment found that the demobilization and reinsertion phases largely achieved their immediate stabilization objectives, with beneficiaries reporting that the process was safe, transparent, and fair. Reinsertion support reached the intended beneficiaries and helped meet immediate needs, while more than 90% of respondents reported no contact with former commanders and almost all reported no pressure to remobilize, indicating successful disengagement from former military structures. Community acceptance was generally high, with limited stigma and strong social cohesion, contributing to a positive foundation for longer-term reintegration.
